expected.tagline: Wake up as Link in a browser-sized fan crossover.
expected.description: An unofficial, free Zelda/Pokémon-inspired browser fan project beginning at the Shrine of Resurrection. Play with keyboard controls and automatic browser saves. Important: the site says saves are deleted after a week without play. No standalone installer or verified native gamepad support is offered.

qualityBar.verdict: Zeldamon offers an easily opened fan crossover in the browser, but its week-long inactivity save limit is a serious caveat for occasional players.

expected.longDescription:
Zeldamon puts its crossover premise on the title screen: a pixel-art fan project drawing on The Legend of Zelda and Pokémon, opened directly in a browser. Its opening message places Link at the Shrine of Resurrection with the Great Plateau outside. That is the invitation to investigate, rather than a claim that this is an official entry in either series or a complete replacement for one.

The immediate appeal is the small distance between curiosity and trying it. There is no separate Windows setup wizard, store client, or emulator configuration in the documented web route. The page loads the game area and keeps a short control guide beneath it. Enter starts the game and opens its menu, while the arrow keys or WASD handle movement. Z talks or confirms, X goes back, and Shift sprints. Those are the controls the project actually publishes, so a keyboard is the supported starting point for this listing.

The page also includes a fullscreen button and an F shortcut, useful if the game area feels cramped in an ordinary browser window. Holding Tab activates the documented fast mode. Having those shortcuts alongside the game makes the first visit less of a guessing exercise, particularly for players who expect controller-style confirm and back buttons but are using a keyboard instead. Native gamepad support has not been verified, and PlayBound does not add a controller badge simply because the presentation resembles a console game.

The most important practical detail is saving. The site says progress is saved automatically in the current browser when you leave the game. It also explicitly says that a save not played for a week is deleted. That is a substantial limitation for anyone who likes to return to an RPG after a long break. Do not assume a PlayBound account backs up this save, that switching browsers carries it over, or that a cloud-sync feature exists. None of those promises is made by this listing.

Its fan-project status deserves the same clarity. The page states that it is unaffiliated with Nintendo, Game Freak, Creatures, and The Pokémon Company, and identifies the series names as their respective owners' trademarks. We link to the project's browser page rather than presenting it as an official release or supplying a standalone package. Availability and the project's contents can change independently of PlayBound.

We are including Zeldamon as a small browser discovery for players interested in fan interpretations of familiar worlds. Its opening is easy to reach and its keyboard instructions are explicit. The save-retention rule makes it a poor recommendation for someone expecting a permanent, leisurely campaign, however. Go in with that limitation understood, use the same browser for return visits, and treat the experience as an unofficial project to explore rather than a guaranteed long-term service.
expected.whyWePickedIt: We picked Zeldamon as a browser discovery for players curious about fan-made crossovers. The direct play page and visible control guide make trying it simple. Its automatic browser saves are not a substitute for durable cloud saves: the stated one-week inactivity deletion rule needs to be visible before someone commits to a long playthrough.

set.tagline: Wake one Link in the Shrine, then invite up to three more into the same Hyrule.
set.description: Zeldamon is an unofficial Zelda and Pokémon-inspired browser adventure from @mozetech. Explore with keyboard or touch controls, keep a local browser save, and open a co-op room so friends can join your world with their own Links. The site deletes saves after a week without play; no standalone installer or verified physical-gamepad mode is offered.

min.notes: Modern JavaScript-enabled browser with keyboard or touch input. The project publishes no numerical CPU, GPU, RAM or storage minimum. Co-op needs a network connection; the save is local to the browser.

recommended.notes: No developer-published recommended hardware tier. A physical gamepad mode has not been verified.

qualityBar.verdict: The shrine opens quickly and a friend can join your Hyrule, but a week's absence can erase the local save.

set.longDescription:
Zeldamon opens with a familiar invitation: Link wakes in the Shrine of Resurrection and the Great Plateau waits outside. The game wears Zelda and Pokémon influences openly, building its adventure in chunky pixel art inside a browser canvas. It is an unofficial fan project, not an entry endorsed by either series owner. The title screen makes that boundary clear, and it gives you the useful controls before asking you to start.

The first stretch has a simple pleasure: press Enter, move with arrows or WASD, and use Z to talk or confirm. X backs out, Shift sprints, and the fullscreen button makes the compact pixel world easier to read. We reached the shrine in a current browser and captured the game's own title art and gameplay for this page. That verifies startup and the first room, not the length or completeness of the wider adventure. The small scale invites curiosity; it does not by itself prove that every part of the world is finished.

There is more to the live build than the previous solo-only listing said. Its loaded co-op module exposes a HOST room and a JOIN flow, with a code that friends can enter from the title screen. The network code assigns separate slots and records for up to four players, each appearing as a Link with their own name and outfit in the host's world. The host keeps the world save. The module also includes chat and a join snapshot so a guest can arrive in the current state rather than restarting the adventure. These are documented behaviors in the game's live code; PlayBound has not yet completed a two-device play test or integrated its room code into a PlayBound party.

That distinction matters when inviting somebody. This is browser co-op through the game's own relay, not a dedicated server or a virtual LAN tunnel. The host opens the room in game and shares its code; guests choose JOIN CO-OP and enter that code. No separate game download is needed, and there is no PlayBound-hosted server package. Keyboard and touch controls are present, but the current input module does not document a physical controller path. A controller-shaped touch overlay is not proof of a gamepad implementation.

Saving is the biggest reason to approach the game carefully. The site says it saves to the current browser when you leave and deletes saves after a week without play. Neither signing in to PlayBound nor inviting a co-op guest turns that into a cloud backup. Keep the same browser for return visits, and do not plan a leisurely campaign around a save that may disappear after a quiet week.

We are reviewing Zeldamon for its quick entry and the surprise of a shared fan-made Hyrule. The co-op implementation makes it more interesting than the old page suggested. Its save limit and unverified longer-term progression keep it in Draft while we test whether the adventure holds together beyond the shrine.
set.whyWePickedIt: We are reviewing Zeldamon because it opens a colorful fan-made Hyrule directly in a browser and lets friends join the host's world as separate Links. We verified the title screen, shrine start and co-op code path; a full two-device test and the one-week save limit still matter before release.
